newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Supreme Court sides with state on abortion law.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Supreme Court sides with state on abortion law.

text.p: A divided Supreme Court Monday set aside a ruling against a 1995 Montana state law that barred physicians' assistants from performing abortions.

At issue was a U.S. appeals court ruling that a federal judge in Montana had erred in assuming the law had the legitimate function of protecting women's health and had a purpose other than making abortions more difficult to obtain.

The high court, by a vote of 6-3, set aside the appeals court ruling and sent the case back for more proceedings. It said 40 other states have similar laws restricting abortions to licensed physicians.

The justices in the unsigned opinion said the appeals court was wrong because the high court in the past has upheld this restriction. The court's most liberal members, Justices John Paul Stevens, Ruth Bader Ginsburg and Stephen Breyer dissented, saying the appeal could have been denied.

"When one looks at the totality of circumstances surrounding the legislation, there is evidence from which one could conclude that the legislature's predominant motive was to make abortions more difficult," Stevens said.
Abortion rights advocates denounced the ruling.

"Today, some of our worst fears about the limits of constitutional protection for women's reproductive health care decisions have come true," said Janet Benshoof of the Centre for Reproductive Law and Policy in New York.

"A majority of the high court has said that an abortion restriction that is designed to limit access to abortion -- not protect women's health or promote informed choices -- is constitutional. This ruling is bad news for women, for doctors and for the Constitution," she said.

In another case, the Supreme Court rejected Utah's appeal of a ruling that struck down as unconstitutional a key section of a 1991 state law banning most abortions after 20 weeks of pregnancy. The court let stand a 1996 U.S. appeals court ruling that the restriction unduly burdens a woman's right to choose an abortion under a 1992 Supreme Court precedent.

The section of the law bans abortions after 20 weeks of pregnancy except in cases of rape or incest, or when necessary to save a woman's life, to prevent "grave damage" to her health or to prevent the birth of a child with grave defects.
Another part of the law, which banned abortions during the first 20 weeks of pregnancy, was struck down earlier and not at issue in the appeals court ruling.

The law had been challenged in court by health care providers in 1991 and has never gone into effect. The appeals court held that the restriction involved an improper "legislative judgment" on when a foetus may be considered viable and said the determination should be left to a physician's medical judgment in each case.

Utah Solicitor General Carol Clawson appealed to the Supreme Court, defending the abortion restriction as constitutional and saying it does not burden a woman's right to choose an abortion earlier in her pregnancy.

"The line drawn by the Utah legislature is consistent with the notion (in the 1992 Supreme Court ruling) that a woman who fails to exercise her right to choose an abortion before viability has consented to the state's intervention on behalf of her developing child," she said.
